sections.authorBiography: Jane Austen was born on 16 December 1775 at Steventon rectory in Hampshire, the seventh of eight children of the Reverend George Austen and Cassandra Leigh Austen. Apart from brief schooling she was educated at home, in a lively family that read novels aloud and staged plays; two of her brothers became admirals in the Royal Navy. She wrote comic pieces as a teenager and drafted the novel that became Pride and Prejudice, then called "First Impressions," in 1796–97. After years in Bath and Southampton she settled in 1809 at Chawton, Hampshire, where she revised and published her novels anonymously: Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814) and Emma (1815). She never married (in 1802 she accepted a proposal from Harris Bigg-Wither and withdrew her acceptance the next day). She died in Winchester on 18 July 1817, aged 41, and is buried in Winchester Cathedral; Northanger Abbey and Persuasion appeared after her death.
sections.historicalContext: The novel is set among the English landed gentry around the turn of the nineteenth century, during the long wars with Revolutionary and Napoleonic France; that is why a militia regiment is quartered at Meryton. Wealth came mainly from land, and estates were often "entailed": settled so that they passed down the male line. Mr. Bennet's estate is entailed on his nearest male relative, so his five daughters will lose their home when he dies. Respectable women of this class could not enter professions, so marriage was the main route to financial security; the novel's money figures (Darcy's £10,000 a year, Elizabeth's expected £1,000 capital) were real stakes. Austen writes in the tradition of the novel of manners, where small social behaviours (who dances with whom, who calls on whom) reveal character and class.

publicationAndReception.publication: Austen's father offered "First Impressions" to the publisher Thomas Cadell in 1797; it was declined by return of post without being read. Revised and retitled, it was sold to Thomas Egerton for £110 and published on 28 January 1813 in three volumes, "By the Author of Sense and Sensibility." Austen called it "my own darling child" in a letter to her sister Cassandra the next day.
publicationAndReception.then: The book was well received: reviews in The British Critic and The Critical Review in 1813 praised its characterization, especially Elizabeth, and the first edition sold out within months, with a second that autumn. Not every later writer was charmed: Charlotte Brontë, in an 1848 letter to G. H. Lewes, found it "a carefully fenced, highly cultivated garden" with "no open country."
publicationAndReception.now: Pride and Prejudice is one of the best-loved novels in English, continuously in print and adapted many times, most famously in the 1995 BBC series and the 2005 film. Critics read it as a comedy of manners, a study of economic pressure on women, and a novel about how we judge other people; its opening sentence is among the most quoted in literature. Austen's portrait appeared on the Bank of England £10 note in 2017, the bicentenary of her death.

sections.overview: Mrs. Bennet is determined to marry off her five daughters; when wealthy Mr. Bingley and his proud friend Mr. Darcy arrive in the neighbourhood, the second daughter, the quick-witted Elizabeth, forms a strong opinion of Darcy at their first meeting. The novel follows the Bennet sisters through balls, visits, letters, a charming officer and a ridiculous clergyman, as Elizabeth learns how much her first impressions were worth.

sections.whyItMatters: The novel is about judging people too quickly, something social media has made more relevant, not less. It also shows clearly how money and law shaped women's lives, and its comedy shows students that serious ideas can be very funny.

spoilerOverview.text: Darcy proposes and is refused; his letter reveals Wickham's true character and Darcy's role in separating Bingley from Jane. Elizabeth realizes her prejudice; at Pemberley she sees a changed Darcy. Lydia elopes with Wickham; Darcy secretly pays to make them marry. Bingley returns and marries Jane; Lady Catherine's attempt to prevent a match backfires, and Darcy and Elizabeth marry.

passage.quote: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife
passage.use: The famous ironic opening: it states a "universal" truth that is really the wish of mothers with daughters. Teach the irony now; the whole novel depends on hearing it.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife” slowly and put it in my own words: The narrator announces that everyone agrees a rich single man must want a wife. Next, craft. I notice the grand, philosophical phrase "a truth universally acknowledged" attached to local gossip, which is irony: the claim is the reverse of the truth. The strongest word is “universally”: it pretends the idea is shared by all the world, when it is really the hope of mothers with daughters. Then, effect. What does Austen's famous first sentence really mean? My answer: It is really the families of unmarried daughters who "want" the rich man; Austen opens by mocking a society where marriage is a matter of money, which is the world the Bennet sisters must survive in.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Austen published Pride and Prejudice in 1813, in a Regency England where estates like Longbourn were often entailed to male heirs, so a gentleman's daughters could be left with little money. Why would marriage matter so much to women in Austen's world? Answer: Accept answers such as: women could rarely own property or work in professions; marriage was the main path to security; the Longbourn entail to Mr. Collins could leave the Bennet daughters with nothing.

criticalVoices.quote: Also read again, and for the third time at least, Miss Austen's very finely written novel of _Pride and Prejudice_. That young lady had a talent for describing the involvements and feelings and characters of ordinary life, which is to me the most wonderful I ever met with. The Big Bow-wow strain I can do myself like any now going; but the exquisite touch, which renders ordinary commonplace things and characters interesting, from the truth of the description and the sentiment, is denied to me. What a pity such a gifted creature died so early!
criticalVoices.speaker: Walter Scott, novelist
criticalVoices.source: The Journal of Sir Walter Scott, entry for 14 March 1826, entry of 14 March 1826
criticalVoices.useNote: Bell-ringer: the bestselling novelist of his age says he cannot do what Austen does. What is the "Big Bow-wow strain," and why might "ordinary commonplace things" be harder to write?
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Describe Austen's reception and what makes "ordinary life" a subject for great fiction.

criticalVoices.quote: Jane Austen's books, too, are absent from this library.  Just that one omission alone would make a fairly good library out of a library that hadn't a book in it.
criticalVoices.speaker: Mark Twain, novelist and humorist
criticalVoices.source: Following the Equator (1897), Chapter LXII, Chapter LXII
criticalVoices.useNote: Four-corners debate with Scott (journal), Brontë and Macaulay: rank the four verdicts and defend the ranking with one passage from Chapter I.
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Weigh dissenting views of Austen (then and now).

lessonPlan.edition: Standard Ebooks edition (from the Project Gutenberg transcription); first published 1813 by Thomas Egerton, London

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Pride and Prejudice.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Pride and Prejudice: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Pride and Prejudice has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to first impressions and prejudice.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Pride and Prejudice. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this chapter, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the chapter on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the chapter to first impressions and prejudice.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the chapter quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Pride and Prejudice.

essentialQuestions: What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about first impressions and prejudice?
What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about pride and self-knowledge?
What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about marriage and money?
What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about class and social mobility?
What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about women's limited choices?
objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the novel in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the chapter quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

items.prompt: Evaluate this claim about the chapter: “Darcy's secret rescue proves his character more than any speech could.” Is it fully persuasive? Argue with evidence, including a passage that complicates it.

scoringGuide.full: 4 points: all four criteria met.
scoringGuide.partial: 3: one criterion missing; 2: two missing; 1: a judgment with no usable evidence.
scoringGuide.zero: 0: off-text, restates the claim, or blank.
criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).
Support: one accurate, located quotation that supports the claim, with explanation (1 point).
Complication: one accurate, located quotation that cuts against the claim (ideally the passage named in the key), explained (1 point).
Qualified conclusion: weighs the support against the complication and says how the claim must be limited (1 point).

Mr. Bennet asks whether his compliments are "the result of previous study," and Collins admits they are; the narrator then notes that "Mr. Bennet's expectations were fully answered.".

The narrator's verdict. The words “Mr. Collins was not a sensible man, and the deficiency of nature had been but little assisted by education or society” (Chapter XV, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops first impressions: Wickham's charm is all surface, and Elizabeth is charmed. Collins switches brides "while Mrs. Bennet was stirring the fire," treating the daughters as interchangeable, while Wickham's "appearance was greatly in his favour," which is all Elizabeth knows of him.

Comic speed: marriage as a choice among interchangeable daughters. The words “Mr. Collins had only to change from Jane to Elizabeth—and it was soon done—done while Mrs. Bennet was stirring the fire” (Chapter XV, paragraph 4) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops first impressions: Wickham's charm is all surface, and Elizabeth is charmed. Collins switches brides "while Mrs. Bennet was stirring the fire," treating the daughters as interchangeable, while Wickham's "appearance was greatly in his favour," which is all Elizabeth knows of him.

Elizabeth's mortification. The words “had her family made an agreement to expose themselves as much as they could during the evening” (Chapter XVIII, paragraph 71) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops family and reputation: the Bennets "expose themselves," as Elizabeth puts it. Elizabeth herself thinks it seemed "her family made an agreement to expose themselves as much as they could," which explains why Darcy fears for Bingley.

Elizabeth insists Jane's loss was caused by "the interference of friends," not chance: an accurate suspicion of Darcy. The words “We do not suffer by accident” (Chapter XXV, paragraph 7) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops marriage and money: Mrs. Gardiner's advice is prudent rather than romantic. Mr. Gardiner is "a sensible, gentleman-like man, greatly superior to his sister," though he lives by trade, and his wife gives Elizabeth the wisest advice in the chapter.

Aristocratic pride in its purest form. The words “Chapter XXIX” (Chapter XXIX, paragraph 36) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops pride and prejudice: aristocratic pride in its purest form. Lady Catherine tells her she gives "your opinion very decidedly for so young a person," a rebuke for not deferring, and Elizabeth goes on doing it.

The cause of separation. The words “there were some very strong objections against the lady” (Chapter XXXIII, paragraph 30) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops marriage and money: even an earl's son must consider fortune. He says Darcy congratulated himself on "having lately saved a friend from the inconveniences of a most imprudent marriage," which Elizabeth instantly understands as Jane's ruin.

The colonel on money. The words “Younger sons cannot marry where they like” (Chapter XXXIII, paragraph 12) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops marriage and money: even an earl's son must consider fortune. He says Darcy congratulated himself on "having lately saved a friend from the inconveniences of a most imprudent marriage," which Elizabeth instantly understands as Jane's ruin.

Moment of recognition. The words “Till this moment, I never knew myself” (Chapter XXXVI, paragraph 8) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops pride and prejudice: Elizabeth sees that vanity, not reason, guided her. She realizes she was "pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect of the other," and concludes, "Till this moment I never knew myself.".

The quiet opening after the storm. The words “The two gentlemen left Rosings the next morning” (Chapter XXXVII, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops pride and prejudice: Elizabeth now feels the justice of Darcy's objections to her family. She now sees that her father, "contented with laughing at them, would never exert himself to restrain the wild giddiness of his youngest daughters," which is Darcy's objection in her own words.

Key line. The words “One has got all the goodness, and the other all the appearance of it” (Chapter XL, paragraph 15) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops first impressions: the sisters debate what to do with what they know. She tells Jane that "one has got all the goodness, and the other all the appearance of it," reversing her earlier judgment of Darcy and Wickham.

Elizabeth's warning. The words “Our importance, our respectability in the world, must be affected by the wild volatility” (Chapter XLI, paragraph 18) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops family and reputation: the father's failure to act sets up the crisis. He admits "Lydia will never be easy till she has exposed herself," yet lets her go because "we shall have no peace at Longbourn" otherwise.

Direct evidence that Darcy's manners have changed; note the list of what has vanished. The words “Never, even in the company of his dear friends at Netherfield, or his dignified relations at Rosings, had she seen him so desirous to…” (Chapter XLIV, paragraph 10) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops pride and prejudice: Darcy has answered her charge of ungentlemanlike behaviour by changing his manners, and she recognizes it. She has never seen him "so desirous to please, so free from self-consequence," and her response is "gratitude ... for loving her still well enough, to forgive all the petulance and acrimony" of her refusal; her feeling rests on what he has done.

Darcy has answered her charge of ungentlemanlike behaviour by changing his manners, and she recognizes it. The words “Chapter XLIV” (Chapter XLIV, paragraph 10) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops pride and prejudice: Darcy has answered her charge of ungentlemanlike behaviour by changing his manners, and she recognizes it. She has never seen him "so desirous to please, so free from self-consequence," and her response is "gratitude ... for loving her still well enough, to forgive all the petulance and acrimony" of her refusal; her feeling rests on what he has done.

Collins's letter: hypocrisy dressed as piety. The words “The death of your daughter would have been a blessing in comparison of this” (Chapter XLVIII, paragraph 12) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops family and reputation: Collins says Lydia's death "would have been a blessing" by comparison: the society's harshest view, made grotesque. He says "let me once in my life feel how much I have been to blame" and adds "it will pass away soon enough," honest about both his guilt and his character.

Her vanity in the title. The words “to hear herself called “Mrs. Wickham,” (Chapter LI, paragraph 10) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops family and reputation: Lydia's shamelessness is complete. "Lydia was Lydia still; untamed, unabashed, wild, noisy, and fearless," and she longs to hear herself called "Mrs. Wickham," prizing the title over the man.

Mrs. Gardiner's hint about love. The words “If he had another motive, I am sure it would never disgrace him” (Chapter LII, paragraph 3) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops pride and prejudice: Darcy has overcome his pride in the most practical way: by binding himself to Wickham as a brother-in-law. Mrs. Gardiner writes that "he had been some days in town before he was able to discover them," and hints that "another motive" would "never disgrace him," which Elizabeth understands as herself.

Mrs. Bennet's excitement: repetition is her voice. The words “He is come—Mr. Bingley is come” (Chapter LV, paragraph 7) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops marriage and money: a marriage of affection and fortune both. She calls herself "the most fortunate creature that ever existed" and asks "why am I thus singled from my family," showing humility even in triumph.

Darcy's self-knowledge. The words “I have been a selfish being all my life, in practice, though not in principle” (Chapter LVIII, paragraph 24) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops pride and prejudice: both acknowledge their faults. Darcy says "my affections and wishes are unchanged, but one word from you will silence me," and admits "I have been a selfish being all my life.".

Jane's question. The words “My dear Lizzy, where can you have been walking to” (Chapter LIX, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops marriage and money: Mr. Bennet warns against an unequal marriage. He warns that she "could be neither happy nor respectable, unless you truly esteemed your husband," and, once convinced, says "I could not have parted with you, my Lizzy, to anyone less worthy.".

finalPaper.title: Pride and Prejudice: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how Jane Austen develops first impressions and prejudice across Pride and Prejudice. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Pride and Prejudice and argue how its meaning changes over the novel and why that change matters to pride and self-knowledge.
Analyze a central character's choices in Pride and Prejudice. Argue whether the novel judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.

Two readers disagree about whether Pride and Prejudice finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of marriage and money. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the chapter and paragraph (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

criticalVoices.quote: The catastrophe, however, is happy, and we are left in doubt whether it would have been better for her or not, to accept the first proposal; and this we conceive is precisely the proper medium; for, though we would not have prudential calculations the sole principle to be regarded in marriage, we are far from advocating their exclusion.
criticalVoices.speaker: Richard Whately (attrib.; the review is unsigned), logician and later Archbishop of Dublin
criticalVoices.source: Review of Northanger Abbey and Persuasion, The Quarterly Review (January 1821), reprinted in Famous Reviews, ed. R. Brimley Johnson (1914), "Archbishop Whately on Jane Austen"
criticalVoices.useNote: Whately on Austen's method: this 1821 review discusses Northanger Abbey and Persuasion, and "her" is Persuasion's Anne Elliot, not Elizabeth Bennet. Use it as a period critic's general principle about prudence in Austen's marriages, not as a comment on this novel. Period voice for the "endorses" side: Whately (writing on Persuasion's Anne Elliot) wants prudence in marriage but not only prudence. Test that "proper medium" against Charlotte Lucas (Ch. XXII), Lydia (Ch. XLVI-L) and Elizabeth's answer to Jane about Pemberley (Ch. LIX). Note for students: "her" is Anne Elliot, not Elizabeth.
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Final paper Prompt 4: weigh whether the novel endorses or criticizes its society's view of marriage and money.
